newsitem.title: GERMANY: Waigel rounds on German SPD tax cut plans.
newsitem.headline: Waigel rounds on German SPD tax cut plans.

text.p: German Finance Minister Theo Waigel on Tuesday rejected as misguided new tax reform proposals unveiled by the opposition Social Democrats (SPD) aimed at pressuring Bonn to cut income taxes even earlier than planned.
Waigel, who insists an overall tax reform cannot go ahead before 1999, said the SPD plan would overburden the better off and do nothing to help lighten the tax load for business.
Chancellor Helmut Kohl's chief of staff, Friedrich Bohl, dismissed it as "cackling and unlaid eggs" and said the SPD's call for all-party tax reform talks was not an honest proposal.

Waigel said the SPD plan, which would lower tax brackets for wage-earners in 1998 and close many loopholes dear to the wealthy, would not simplify the complex tax system. It also did not spell out how to make up for the 50 billion mark ($33.6 billion) revenue shortfall it would create, he said.
"The SPD proposals are not a comprehensive tax policy," Waigel said in a statement. "People who already have a high tax burden would end up footing the bill."
The two mens' reactions, the latest shots in a mounting debate over Germany's heavy tax burden, contrasted with that of Kohl's liberal coalition partners.
The Free Democrats (FDP), who are also pressing for tax reform in 1998, welcomed the plan even though they favour deeper cuts for business and the better off.
"I'm very pleased the SPD is now moving on tax policy," FDP general secretary Guido Westerwelle told ARD television.

The tax reform the SPD party executive on Monday would help average wage-earners by cutting the starting tax rate to 19.5 percent from 25.9 percent and boosting the standard personal deduction from 12,000 marks ($8,066) to 14,000 marks.
The plan, which commentators hailed as a smart tactical move, would also close many of the countless loopholes clever tax advisors use to lighten the tax load for the wealthy.
The proposal came after a month of verbal brawling in Bonn between the FDP and Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU) over the date for the long-awaited reform.

The SPD pointedly left open the issue of lowering the peak tax rate of 53 percent, saying it still had to see how much new revenue was needed from higher-bracket taxpayers to help make up for the 50 billion marks lost through the reform.
"I don't want to talk about a peak rate because that depends on how many loopholes we can close," SPD finance expert Ingrid Matthaeus-Meier told the Sueddeutsche Zeitung.

Waigel has already said Bonn wants to cut the minimum tax rate to around 20 percent and drop the ceiling to under 40 percent. The government plan would also close loopholes, although none have been identified so far.
It should be passed into law during 1997 but not take effect until after the general election planned for late 1998.

Kohl has said Germany probably had to raise value-added tax sometime in future but promised this would not happen before 1999. VAT is currently 15 percent on most items and both the FDP and the SPD are firmly against raising it.
Handelsblatt, Germany's business daily, said the SPD had succeeded in taking the initiative in the tax debate.
"All other tax plans presented in the coming months will have to judged in comparison to these SPD proposals," the newspaper wrote in an editorial entitled "Tactical Advantage."
"That goes especially for the tax proposals of the Bonn coalition due at the end of this year," it wrote.
